summary: Across 1,000 simulated futures, buying the $800 laptop changes Alex's median projected balance on 2027-05-01 from $3,396 to $2,596 (middle 80% of futures: $2,117 to $3,100). Alex meets the $1,600 summer housing goal on top of the $1,500 emergency reserve in 10% of futures with the purchase, versus 77% without it. Checking falls below the $200 low-balance line in 97% of futures, versus 2% without it. Total savings dip below the $1,500 emergency reserve in 18% of futures, versus 0%. In 51% of futures Alex would have to move money out of savings to pay a mandatory bill, versus 0% without the purchase. A dated low point takes a single run: on the expected-value path, checking bottoms out at -$26 on 2027-01-01, versus $769 in the baseline.

drivers.label: Laptop (this purchase)
drivers.detail: The purchase being simulated: a one-time $800 from Everyday Checking on 2026-09-20. It happens in one scenario only.

drivers.label: Lowest checking balance
drivers.detail: Across the 1,000 simulated futures, the median low point for checking is -$31, versus $708 in the baseline.

drivers.label: Summer housing goal
drivers.detail: In the median future, $1,096 is available for the $1,600 goal on 2027-05-01 after the reserve, versus $1,896.

drivers.label: Busy spending stretch
drivers.detail: The laptop on 2026-09-20 lands at the start of a busy stretch: everyday spending through 2026-10-03 is expected to be $319, versus $259 in an average stretch of the year (groceries: 1.26× usual; discretionary: 1.19× usual). This happens with or without the purchase.

drivers.label: Expected income
drivers.detail: $11,603 of expected income through 2027-05-01 rebuilds the balance in both scenarios.

assumptions: Precomputed result: generated by the Monte Carlo simulator (seed 1) for this $800 laptop request; it does not respond to other requests.
We compared 1,000 possible futures. Each future uses the same paycheck and spending changes for the baseline and purchase, so the purchase is the only difference.
Balances show the middle result across those futures. Probabilities show how often an event happened.
Paychecks vary around their expected amounts using the uncertainty recorded in the twin. Extreme values are capped, and paychecks cannot be negative.

Each spending category varies independently every two weeks using its expected amount and uncertainty. The two-week total is spread evenly across its days; values below $0 are treated as $0, which nudges average spending upward.
Spending estimates use 25 two-week periods observed from 2025-10-04 to 2026-09-18. Recent periods count more; a period 180 days older gets half the weight.
Seasonal categories adjust their typical spending and likely range for the time of year. A two-week period that crosses months blends both months, while the yearly average stays unchanged.
Groceries spending is usually highest in January (1.63× its typical two-week amount) and lowest in July (0.60×).
Discretionary spending is usually highest in December (2.34× its typical two-week amount) and lowest in April (0.49×).
Bill amounts, bill due dates, and paycheck dates are fixed; bill confidence is not used.
A mandatory bill checking cannot cover is paid by moving money from savings, even if that breaks the emergency reserve; it counts as uncovered only when checking and savings together fall short.
Everyday spending and optional charges are never paid from savings.
Low balance means checking below $200 (default; Alex has not set a minimum).
The emergency reserve counts checking plus savings.
Goals must be met on top of the emergency reserve.
Income, bills, and everyday spending all flow through checking.
Every active recurring bill, including optional ones, is charged in full.
